column4: A speaker calls God to witness what is in his heart while his conduct makes him the fiercest adversary; claimed inward testimony and the person's true condition sharply diverge.
People say they believe with their mouths while their hearts have not believed and they eagerly listen to falsehood; speech and hearing expose no reliable knowledge of the interior.
The hypocrites fear a surah that will inform them of what is in their hearts, and God promises to bring out what they fear; concealed interior becomes disclosed report.

God has already informed the believers of the absentees' reports, will see their deeds, and will return them to the Knower of unseen and seen who informs them; report, seeing, knowledge, and final disclosure form one sequence.

Those who deny the Hour are answered by the Knower of the unseen, from whom not even an atom is hidden and in whose clear record everything remains; resurrection and exhaustive knowledge meet directly.
At judgment every soul knows what it sent ahead and is returned to God, so the person's history becomes fully known only at its destination.
God knows what people conceal and reveal, a repeated direct formulation of the section's exterior-to-interior movement.
Abraham addresses the Lord as knowing what people conceal and reveal and says nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from God.
The messenger's task is communication, while God knows what people reveal and conceal; human informing and divine interior knowledge are expressly distinguished.
In the setting of secretly extending affection to enemies, God says He knows what people conceal and disclose; the hidden allegiance behind an outward act is known.
Whether people disclose or conceal anything, God knows all things, restating the section's boundary between visible expression and divine knowledge.
God is the Manifest and the Hidden and knows everything; the ayah places outwardness, inwardness, and knowledge in one compact formulation.
The Prophet conceals within himself what God will disclose; the ayah directly stages an interior fact becoming outward under divine knowledge.
Joseph keeps a response within himself and does not reveal it to his brothers, while God is invoked as knowing their description; human concealment and divine knowledge are juxtaposed.
God knows what people harbor within themselves even when a matter is kept as a secret promise, making the self's unspoken content the object of knowledge.
God knows what lies in the hypocrites' hearts and commands speech addressed to their very selves; outward admonition is grounded in knowledge of their interior.
Humanity answers the primordial question with بَلَىٰ شَهِدْنَا so that no one can claim unawareness on resurrection; self-testimony is set directly against later ignorance.
The possible excuse that ancestors associated others with God cannot cancel the testimony of 7:172, paralleling the section's self-witness that survives offered excuses.
A witness is drawn from every community, the people are challenged for proof, and then they know that truth belongs to God; judgment moves from testimony to conclusive knowledge.
Believers must verify rather than tell a person offering peace that he is not a believer, and God is fully aware of deeds; human sight cannot safely pronounce on inward faith.
A lived test makes known who truly strives without hidden intimates besides God, and the ayah ends with God as aware of what people do; conduct discloses inner allegiance.
Reachable game serves as a test so that God makes known who fears Him unseen; trial exposes an inward fear that cannot itself be viewed.
The change of direction serves to make known who follows the messenger and who turns back; an observable response to trial discloses allegiance.
The question denies entry into the Garden before the strivers and steadfast are made known; trial reveals the reality behind aspiration.
Revelation, balance, and iron are given so that God makes known who supports Him and His messengers unseen; outward aid discloses an inward stance.
Death and life are created as a test of who is best in deed, supplying the experiential testing behind the same surah's declaration that the Creator is خبِير in 67:14.
The people of the Fire say that if they had listened or reasoned they would not be among its inhabitants; hearing joined to understanding would have grasped the destination they missed.
Some listen to the Prophet and then ask knowledgeable hearers what he just said; hearing has occurred without knowledge because their hearts are sealed.
Those who listen to speech and follow its best meaning are the people of understanding; this is a positive instance of hearing becoming discerning knowledge.
The person given his record in the right hand invites others to read it, turning his entire history into visible, communicable evidence.
He says he had known he would meet his reckoning, contrasting true prior knowledge of destination with the failure exposed in the section's question.
The condemned person had thought he would never return, precisely stating a failure to grasp where his visible life would lead.
The denial is answered that his Lord was always seeing him; deficient human forecast is set against continuous divine sight of the person.
At judgment there appears to the wrongdoers from God what they had never reckoned with; the consequence hidden behind their visible condition becomes manifest.
The evils they earned become visible to them and surround them, completing the movement from ungrasped outcome to inescapable sight.
The evils of people's deeds become visible and what they mocked surrounds them; an inwardly discounted destination becomes witnessed reality.
On the day every soul finds its good and evil deeds present, the person's moral interior history stands visibly before it.
What people had concealed before becomes manifest, a direct disclosure of hidden reality despite the false promise they then voice.
On the day a person remembers what he strove for, his own history returns as knowledge at judgment.
Hell is made plainly visible to everyone who sees, giving visible outcome to the remembered striving of 79:35.
When Hell is brought near, the person remembers, but the ayah asks what use that late remembrance can have; knowledge arrives only with the seen consequence.
The person wishes he had sent something ahead for his life, articulating too late the destination he failed to grasp beforehand.
God records what people send ahead and the آثار they leave, enumerating everything in a clear register; the person's full trace is preserved for later report.
A record speaks with truth and no soul is wronged; written evidence functions as the decisive report of the person's acts.
Everything people did is preserved in written records, preventing their own forgetting or concealment from erasing the truth.
Every small and great thing is inscribed, completing the records' exhaustive knowledge of a person's history.
God already knows the state people are upon, and on the day they return He informs them of what they did; knowledge concerns their condition before it becomes final report.
God takes people by night, knows what they commit by day, raises them until the term, and then informs them of their deeds; hidden life, knowledge, return, and report form a sequence.
Deniers of resurrection are told they will be raised and then informed of what they did; divine report answers their failed knowledge of destination.
The command to ask one who is خَبِير about the Creator presents the fully aware knower as the proper source of reliable report.
Public charity is good and hidden charity better, while God is aware of what people do; different visibility to humans does not change divine knowledge.
Some listen while coverings lie over their hearts so they do not understand and heaviness is in their ears; sensory presence fails to become knowledge.
Coverings over hearts prevent understanding and heaviness in ears prevents reception even while the recitation is heard, separating audition from inward grasp.
One reminded of God's signs turns away while coverings over hearts and heaviness in ears prevent understanding; visible and audible reminder does not ensure knowledge.
God knows what lies within breasts in the context of a dream-image that shapes courage and dispute; divine interior knowledge governs a limited human perception.
God's knowledge of good within captives' hearts determines a better gift, making hidden inward quality rather than visible captivity decisive.
The question asks whether the hearer knows that God knows all in heaven and earth and that it is in a record; human knowledge is redirected toward divine recorded knowledge.
People are told to leave both the apparent and hidden forms of sin because both will be recompensed; moral interior and exterior reach the same destination.
When people see divine punishment they finally profess belief and reject former partners; sight produces acknowledgment only after the outcome arrives.
Faith does not benefit them once they have seen the punishment, marking the boundary between timely knowledge and certainty forced by the final scene.
At the trumpet people rush from their graves to their Lord, continuing the grave-opening scene that follows the section's knowledge-question.
Those emerging ask who raised them, and the answer identifies the promised resurrection; bewildered perception precedes informed recognition.
